questions.prompt: 왁글 댄스에서 춤의 각도가 나타내는 것은?
questions.explain: angle → direction relative to the sun.
questions.passage: When a honeybee discovers a rich source of nectar, it returns to the hive and performs what scientists call a 'waggle dance.' The dance conveys remarkably precise information: the angle of the dance relative to the vertical comb indicates the direction of the food source relative to the sun, while the duration of the waggle phase signals the distance. Bees watching the dance in the darkness of the hive read these signals through touch and vibration rather than sight. Experiments in which researchers moved feeding stations confirmed that recruits flew to the locations encoded in the dance, not simply to places with floral scent. The waggle dance is therefore often cited as one of the few examples of symbolic communication in non-human animals.

questions.passage: Modern concrete typically begins to crack within decades, yet many Roman structures, including harbors exposed to seawater for two thousand years, remain intact. The Romans mixed volcanic ash with lime and seawater, producing a mineral called aluminous tobermorite as the material aged. Rather than weakening the structure, chemical reactions between seawater and the ash actually reinforced it over time, filling cracks as they formed. Engineers today study this 'self-healing' property in hopes of producing more durable and environmentally friendly building materials, since modern cement production accounts for roughly eight percent of global carbon dioxide emissions.

questions.prompt: 서파 수면 중 해마가 하는 일은?
questions.passage: A growing body of research indicates that sleep plays an active role in consolidating memories. During slow-wave sleep, the hippocampus repeatedly 'replays' patterns of neural activity associated with recent experiences, gradually transferring information to the neocortex for long-term storage. In one influential study, participants who learned word pairs and then slept recalled significantly more pairs than those who remained awake for the same interval. Notably, the benefit was greatest when sleep occurred shortly after learning. These findings challenge the older view of sleep as a passive state and suggest that students who sacrifice sleep to study may be undermining the very process that stabilizes what they have learned.

questions.passage: The introduction of the movable-type printing press in fifteenth-century Europe transformed the economics of knowledge. Before Gutenberg, producing a single book required months of a scribe's labor, making books luxury items owned mainly by monasteries and wealthy elites. Within fifty years of the press's invention, an estimated twenty million volumes had been printed. Falling prices broadened readership, which in turn created incentives for authors to write in vernacular languages rather than Latin. Historians argue that this feedback loop — cheaper books producing more readers producing more books — accelerated the Reformation, the Scientific Revolution, and ultimately the spread of literacy itself.

questions.prompt: 도시가 교외보다 더운 원인이 아닌 것은?
questions.passage: Cities are consistently warmer than the rural areas that surround them, a phenomenon known as the urban heat island effect. Asphalt and concrete absorb solar radiation by day and release it slowly at night, while the scarcity of vegetation reduces cooling through evaporation. Waste heat from vehicles, air conditioners, and industry adds to the burden. The temperature gap, typically one to three degrees Celsius, can exceed ten degrees on calm summer nights. Mitigation strategies include planting street trees, installing reflective 'cool roofs,' and preserving urban parks. Studies show that neighborhoods with abundant tree cover can be several degrees cooler than adjacent districts, which has significant implications for public health during heat waves.

questions.prompt: 베게너의 이론이 수십 년간 거부된 이유는?
questions.explain: could not explain what force moved the continents.
questions.passage: In 1912, Alfred Wegener proposed that the continents had once been joined in a single landmass he called Pangaea. He noted that the coastlines of South America and Africa fit together like puzzle pieces, that identical fossils appeared on both sides of the Atlantic, and that glacial deposits occurred in now-tropical regions. Yet geologists largely rejected his theory for decades because Wegener could not explain what force moved the continents. The mechanism emerged in the 1960s with the theory of plate tectonics: the discovery of seafloor spreading showed that new crust forms at mid-ocean ridges, pushing plates apart at roughly the speed fingernails grow. Wegener's evidence, once dismissed, is now taught as a classic case of data preceding explanation.

questions.passage: Classical economics assumes that individuals weigh costs and benefits rationally, yet behavioral research reveals systematic departures from rationality. People overvalue immediate rewards, follow default options, and are influenced by how choices are framed. 'Nudge' policies exploit these tendencies for public benefit without restricting freedom of choice. When organ donation systems switched from opt-in to opt-out, effective consent rates rose dramatically; when cafeterias placed fruit at eye level, consumption increased. Critics argue that nudging can shade into manipulation, since it operates below conscious awareness. Proponents respond that some choice architecture is unavoidable — every menu has a first item — so designers might as well arrange it to serve people's own long-term interests.

Today we'll look at why eyewitness testimony is less reliable than juries tend to assume. Memory is not a video recording. Each time we recall an event, we actually reconstruct it, and new information can slip into the reconstruction. In a famous experiment, participants watched a car accident. Those asked how fast the cars were going when they 'smashed' into each other reported higher speeds than those who heard the word 'hit.' A week later, the 'smashed' group even remembered seeing broken glass — glass that never existed. This is called the misinformation effect, and it has led many courts to treat eyewitness accounts with greater caution.

Octopuses are masters of disguise, and what makes this remarkable is that they are almost certainly colorblind. Their skin contains thousands of pigment sacs called chromatophores, each controlled by muscles and nerves, which expand or contract to change color in a fraction of a second. Beneath these lie reflective cells that mimic the brightness and texture of the surroundings. So how does a colorblind animal match colors it cannot see? One hypothesis is that light-sensitive proteins in the skin itself allow the octopus to 'see' with its body. The debate is ongoing, but it reminds us that vision, in the broadest sense, need not be confined to eyes.

When we say 'Silk Road,' the singular is misleading. It was a shifting network of caravan routes linking China to the Mediterranean, and silk was only one of many goods. Paper, spices, glassware, and horses moved along it — but so did ideas. Buddhism traveled from India into China along these routes, and centuries later, technologies like papermaking moved west, reaching Europe through the Islamic world. Of course, the network also carried disease; many historians believe the plague of the fourteenth century followed trade routes into Europe. So the Silk Road is best understood not as a road at all, but as history's first great information superhighway — with all the benefits and risks that implies.

Coral reefs cover less than one percent of the ocean floor, yet they support about a quarter of all marine species. The coral animal itself is nearly transparent; its brilliant colors come from microscopic algae living inside its tissues. The algae photosynthesize and share nutrients with the coral — a textbook case of mutualism. But this partnership is temperature-sensitive. When water warms by even one or two degrees for several weeks, corals expel their algae and turn bone white, a process called bleaching. Bleached corals are not dead, but they are starving, and if the heat persists they die. That's why marine biologists treat mass bleaching events as early warning systems for ocean warming.

How do we find planets orbiting stars light-years away, when the star outshines the planet a billion to one? Mostly, we don't look for the planet at all — we watch the star. In the transit method, we measure the star's brightness continuously; if a planet crosses in front, the light dips by a tiny, regular amount. The size of the dip tells us the planet's diameter, and the interval between dips gives its orbital period. The radial velocity method instead watches the star wobble: an orbiting planet tugs its star back and forth, shifting the starlight's color slightly toward blue, then red. Combining both methods yields the planet's density — and that tells us whether we're looking at a gas giant or a rocky world like our own.

questions.explain: light dips by a tiny, regular amount.

In 1874, a group of painters rejected by the official Paris Salon organized their own exhibition. A critic, mocking Monet's 'Impression, Sunrise,' called them mere 'impressionists' — and the insult became a movement's name. What made their work radical? First, they left the studio to paint outdoors, capturing changing light directly. Second, new chemistry gave them portable paint tubes and brighter pigments. Third, they painted modern life — railway stations, cafés, weekend crowds — subjects the academy considered vulgar. Within a generation, the outsiders had redefined what painting could be, and the Salon that rejected them became a historical footnote.

First, they left the studio to paint outdoors, capturing changing light directly. Second, new chemistry gave them portable paint tubes and brighter pigments. Third, they painted modern life — railway stations, cafés, weekend crowds — subjects the academy considered vulgar. Within a generation, the outsiders had redefined what painting could be, and the Salon that rejected them became a historical footnote.
